organic-waste-paper:
A Better Way to Address Urban Organic Waste in NYC
Completed: 2025-12-16
( Back )



Overview
    This is a graduate research report about organic waste in NYC, published for the class URPL-GP 2625, Environment Infrastructure. It explores composting, anaerobic digestion, and waste to energy. Final recommendations are listed below.
    Introduction
    As global populations grow and the demand for energy, food, and water accelerates, the volume of organic waste will rise in parallel. For cities looking to reduce greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions, organic waste is one of the clearest intervention points. In the United States, the entire material economy still funnels more than half of all municipal solid waste into landfills and each of these sites emit methane, a greenhouse gas over 20 times more potent than carbon dioxide (EPA 2019; Rafiee et al. 2021). Much of what ends up in landfills is organic waste (EPA 2019) – food scraps, yard waste, soiled paper and other biodegradable materials that can remain trapped for decades.

    This dependence on landfills is both an environmental liability and a missed circular-economy opportunity. Managed differently, organic waste can instead be used in a much more healthy and productive way for the world. It can return nutrients to soils, generate renewable energy, reduce landfill dependence, and sharply limit climate impacts (Feiz et al. 2020; Chrispim et al. 2021).

    The three most popular alternative landfill approaches are thermal waste-to-energy (WtE), composting, and anaerobic digestion (AD). Each involves tradeoffs across climate performance, public health, equity, cost, and long-term governance. Thermal WtE reduces landfill methane and generates electricity, but carries pollution and siting burdens. Composting delivers strong nutrient recovery and the lowest emissions, but requires clean feedstock and significant space. AD creates both renewable gas and nutrient-rich materials, but depends on sophisticated pre-processing, high capital investment, and sustained interagency coordination.1

    New York City (NYC) sits at a pivotal decision point. It has done much to improve tackling organic waste: expanding community and industrial composting, launching citywide curbside organics collection, piloting AD co-digestion at Newtown Creek, and sending residual waste to regional WtE plants. But all of these approaches remain constrained by the same bottleneck – a sufficient pre-processing capacity to reliably separate, clean, and prepare organics at scale.

    It also reflects long-standing equity and environmental justice concerns. Most of NYC’s existing waste infrastructure has historically been sited or adjacent to low-income communities and communities of color. Thus, any effort to reform organic waste management must be evaluated on its burdens and benefits across surrounding communities.

    This crossroads asks a central planning question: How should New York City evaluate composting, AD, and WtE as strategies for managing organic waste, and what combination of these systems can create a sustainable and circular approach? 

    Answering this question requires a framework that assesses each technology across environmental, social, and economic criteria, drawing on historical and technical research, case studies from U.S. and international cities, and interviews with NYC waste practitioners. Using this framework, the paper offers recommendations for NYC, emphasizing a hybrid system that prioritizes composting and AD, while restricting WtE to a highly regulated, minimal role.

    Evaluating Three Organic Waste Approaches
    Composting, AD, and thermal WtE each have distinct environmental, political, operational, and governance implications. Climate performance depends not only on emissions produced on-site but also on avoided emissions, energy displacement, process efficiency, and long-term risks. This section evaluates composting, AD, and WtE across four sustainability dimensions: climate impact, circular value, infrastructure feasibility, and community equity.

    Composting
    Composting uses aerobic microbial decomposition, a process in which microorganisms convert organic matter into carbon dioxide, water vapor, and stabilized organic carbon. The organic carbon and macronutrients – nitrogen, phosphorus, and potassium – can be used as an alternative fertilizer in soil (NYSDEC 2017). It also produces ammonia and nitrous oxide and other emissions based on moisture, aeration, and carbon-to-nitrogen ratio (Lin et al. 2019). When properly managed, composting consistently demonstrates among the lowest GHG profiles of any organic waste pathway.

    In talking with Arianna Cooper, the Director of Sustainability for Chartwells at NYU, starting a pilot compost program is often much more challenging than scaling a compost program. A pilot program has limited contamination and enthusiastic early adopters, with manageable waste volumes that can be handled by existing processors. But scaling one up across a neighborhood requires much more land and operational expertise. There is a higher likelihood of more contaminants, degrading compost quality and driving up labor and disposal costs (Farrell & Jones 2009).

    In Asia and the Middle East, composting is often a municipal service integrated into the core waste management system (Selvasembian 2024). European and U.S. systems typically use public–private models, where municipalities oversee system design and quality while private operators manage processing. U.S. systems rely more heavily on community-scale composting, creating coordination challenges (NYSDEC 2017).

    Having worked to scale composting across multiple universities and business campuses, Cooper is of the perspective that better regional planning is required to make the most out of composting. And the office of Brooklyn Borough President Antonio Reynoso supports this, indicating that NYC has yet to take advantage of multiple collection methods, including curbside, community drop-offs, and school programs, and regional processes are required to manage smaller volumes and provide more public education (Wallace 2025). Financing is comparatively straightforward, with major costs in site acquisition, equipment, and labor. EPA cost models estimate processing costs at $30–$70 per ton (EPA 1994; EPA WARM 2020), with contamination being a major cost driver (EPA 2020).

    Composting has fewer environmental burdens than AD or WtE, but poorly managed facilities can still create odors, pests, and truck traffic, which Cooper noted is often concentrated in low-income neighborhoods. But she states that if done right, composting can offer unique equity benefits as it is labor-intensive and creates local green jobs . Community stewardship can also be built through school programs, urban agriculture, and neighborhood greening (Pollans 2025).

    Anaerobic Digestion
    AD is an anaerobic bioglocal process, directly contrasting composting, as it intentionally fosters conditions to generate a biogas that can be used for heat, electricity, or upgraded into a renewable natural gas for energy. It can enhance energy resilience by replacing fossil fuels when integrated into the energy grid and existing wastewater treatment plants (Wu et al. 2022).

    Digestate, a nutrient-rich material containing nitrogen, phosphorus, and micronutrients is also produced from the AD process in both a solid and liquid form. The solid digestate then goes through additional post-treatment before becoming compost (Donoso-Bricenao et al. 2021). 

    All of this work for AD is incredibly capital intensive and operationally complex, according to Jennifer McDonnell, the Director of Wastewater Resource Recovery at DSNY. Having researched into AD implementation for DSNY, she identified that digesters, heating systems, and biogas upgrading units require substantial upfront investment. Pre-processing is even more important, as she said that all research points toward source-separated organic waste dramatically improving AD performance and digestate quality. In Abu Dhabi for example, economic viability for AD is heavily reliant on fermentation yields, pre-treatment technologies, and market value for fermentation byproducts (El-Masha et al. 2019).

    Technological advancements do continue to accelerate improving digestate quality and energy yield, with Spanish wastewater treatment plants having shown “significant unrealized biogas potential” due to suboptimal retention times and mixing (Buendía et al. 2015). Yet, this requires ongoing reinvestment in equipment and training (Rafiee et al. 2021; Donoso-Briceno et al. 2021).

    McDonnell also called out that AD demands close coordination across agencies including sanitation, wastewater, environmental, and energy. Pilots often fail to scale due to contamination, variable waste streams, and insufficient pre-processing infrastructure (Buendía et al. 2015). This dynamic is reflected in underperformance in both Spain and Abu Dhabi, where the economic viability of AD was shown to depend heavily on fermentation yields, consistent pre-treatment technologies, and reliable markets for byproducts (El-Mashad et al. 2019). 

    McDonnell has noted that AD facilities are often built with wastewater facilities in low-income communities, which does raise major environmental justice concerns around odors, truck traffic, and cumulative impacts. Climate benefits depend heavily on operational precision as there is also the potential for methane leakage (Xu 2019; Rafiee et al. 2021; Donoso-Briceño et al. 2021). While there is some benefit that can come from AD, the immediate effect is often not seen in the immediate community. Ensuring equity within AD systems requires early community engagement, transparent operations, and clear benefit-sharing mechanisms. 

    Thermal WtE
    WtE combusts mixed municipal waste in high-temperature incinerators, producing electricity while reducing the need for landfills. 

    Yet, while WtE prevents landfill methane, it still emits CO₂, nitrogen oxides, sulfur oxides, and particulates. Organic waste actually performs poorly in WtE systems due to its high moisture content and low calorific value. Wet organics depress furnace temperatures, requiring supplemental fuel or blending with high-energy materials like plastics. Not only that, but combustion destroys nutrients, eliminating any opportunity to recover nitrogen, phosphorus, or carbon. 

    In talking with William Flood, an environmental engineer at Reworld, the company that runs WtE thermal plants in New Jersey, it’s clear that WtE has made drastic improvements over the past several decades. Energy generation is more reliable and dispatchable, an advantage over intermittent renewable resources. Modern European systems incorporate improved combustion controls and sophisticated emissions treatment paired with mechanical-biological treatment (MBT) can remove inerts and improve performance. 

    WtE also produces post-combustion metals, and in rare cases, mineralized ash used for construction aggregate. Reworld’s life-cycle assessment identifies two primary beneficial outputs from WtE: post-combustion metal recovery and fossil energy displacement via electricity generation (Reworld 2025). Recovery of ferrous and non-ferrous metals can be substantial at scale because combustion concentrates metallic content into ash residues, making them easier to extract. 

    Despite its limitations, Flood notes that WtE can play a role as a residual waste technology. Its engineering is optimized for dry, high-calorific materials such as plastics, paper, and textiles. He identifies that combusting organics reduces energy efficiency, and increases fuel demand, so pre-processing is critical to better address organic waste through other methods like composting or AD.

    Pre-processing systems such as MBT or RDF production, however, can also add further infrastructure burdens. These facilities require separators, screens, shredders, dryers, and sometimes biological stabilization tunnels, each with substantial capital and operating costs. Because they introduce additional waste-handling stages, they also trigger separate permitting for air quality, stormwater, worker safety, and residuals management. Oversight becomes fragmented across multiple agencies responsible for waste, energy, and environmental regulation, increasing the risk of compliance gaps. Any failure is highly visible and can lead to significant financial or political fallout.

    The core mass-burn facilities themselves also require hundreds of millions of dollars for combustion units, boilers, turbines, and sophisticated emissions-control systems. These systems must be continually upgraded to meet tightening environmental standards, and facilities rely on long-term contracts guaranteeing minimum waste tonnage. As Syngellakis (2015) notes, mismatches between assumed and actual waste composition can cause costly operational failures, while Reworld (2025) reports frequent unplanned upgrades to pollution-control or ash-handling systems.

    Governance challenges parallel those of AD but with higher financial stakes. Most U.S. WtE facilities operate under public–private hybrid models in which private firms build and run plants while municipalities commit to guaranteed waste flows and regulatory oversight. Although this spreads risk, it also limits flexibility as waste policies evolve. Maintaining community trust remains difficult given the facilities’ scale, emission profiles, and histories of inequitable siting.

    Many of these external burdens fall disproportionately on low-income neighborhoods and communities of color, where many U.S. incinerators have historically been sited. Because WtE infrastructure often coexists with transfer stations, truck routes, warehouses, and other industrial uses, cumulative exposure raises health and equity concerns even where emissions adhere to regulatory limits. If MBT or RDF facilities are added to pre-process organics, they are typically located adjacent to existing WtE sites, further concentrating environmental infrastructure in already overburdened communities (Reworld 2025). Reworld’s sustainability report explicitly acknowledges that community legitimacy depends on transparent air monitoring, proactive engagement, and responsiveness to local concerns.

    Viewed this way, WtE serves as a disposal option for residual waste, but should not be the primary treatment pathway for organic waste. While reliable for dry, high-calorific materials, it performs poorly for organics, offers limited circular benefits, and raises significant equity concerns. Its role in a sustainable waste system is therefore narrow and highly constrained.

    Stakeholder Landscape
    The implementation of composting, AD, and WtE systems is shaped by a diverse set of stakeholders spanning public agencies, private operators, communities, and energy markets. These stakeholders vary in their degree of control over infrastructure siting, financing, operations, and regulatory oversight, and often hold competing priorities regarding cost, environmental performance, and equity outcomes.

    At the center of this landscape are municipal governments and public agencies, including sanitation departments, environmental protection agencies, and wastewater utilities. Each of these entities are directly responsible to meet targets and comply with environmental regulations, all while managing complex budgets. Getting the chance to talk with McDonnell was critical, as she leads Wastewater Recovery and understands the technology required to improve the system and the politics involved with expansion and costs.

    Private waste management and energy operators represent another powerful stakeholder group, particularly in AD and WtE systems. These actors include waste haulers, facility developers, plant operators, and energy utilities. Talking with Flood, an engineer at Reworld, was helpful to better understand new technology development and long-term partnership contracts held with municipal governments, while also being well aware of the politics that come with their work.

    Local communities and residents, especially those directly living near waste processing facilities, are among the most affected stakeholders but often possess the least formal decision-making power. It proved challenging to find someone who lived in these communities who was open to discussion, but chatting with Cooper, the director of sustainability for Chartwells at NYU, who had previous experience working at a nonprofit directly connected with residents, was helpful to understand the historical context in NYC. These communities have a lived experience with the localized impacts of organic waste infrastructure, including truck traffic, air quality concerns, odor, noise, and land use conflicts.

    Other important stakeholders include state and federal regulators, who permit the processes and standards the government is supposed to follow, and the everyday citizen taxpayers, who may care about the budget and our existing waste system. 

    Across all of these stakeholder groups, power is unequally distributed. Municipal agencies and private operators hold the greatest power due to capital planning and contracting, but communities and residents hold the required public approval for these large city projects. This imbalance is evident in the approach toward organic waste technology in NYC today. Rolling out a comprehensive composting program can be just as challenging as upgrading AD due to the amount of coordination, capital, and buy-in required; yet, due to the difference in centralized vs. decentralized locations, certain projects like AD and WtE may be easier for those with power to execute. For example, the recent composting project proposal through Reynoso’s office was originally deemed less feasible by the DSNY, not necessarily because of capital, but because of the coordination required.

    This power dynamic helps better understand in interviews why certain folks, like McDonnell and Flood, preferred approaches where it was easier to execute and more technically focused, and Cooper preferred an approach that was more community oriented. Based on this, organic waste management must not solely be viewed based on technical or environmental criteria, but also review the governance structures, financial incentives and power relationships between stakeholders.

    Rubric for Evaluating Organic Waste Approaches
    Cities evaluating organics management systems require a framework that captures not only environmental performance but also long-term operational, financial, and equity impacts. Drawing from the section above, this paper compares composting, AD, and thermal WtE across the four dimensions of climate impact, circular value, infrastructure feasibility, and environmental justice. These dimensions reveal that each technology operates with distinct tradeoffs, and that their performance depends heavily on governance, feedstock quality, scale, and local policy objectives. 



    Across all four sustainability dimensions, the comparative evaluation reveals that no single technology performs best on all metrics, and that each plays a different role within an integrated organics strategy.

    Composting delivers the strongest circular benefits and the lowest emissions profile but struggles with land constraints, contamination, and scaling in dense cities. Its success depends on consistent public engagement, reliable feedstock quality, and steady market demand for compost. AD provides meaningful climate and energy benefits, but its performance is highly sensitive to operational precision and contamination control. AD requires significant capital investment, advanced technological expertise, and interagency coordination, making it harder to deploy at scale without long-term institutional commitments. Thermal WtE offers reliable electricity generation and reduces landfill methane, but performs weakest on circularity, climate alignment, and equity. WtE infrastructure is expensive, politically constrained, and least suited for organics, making it an appropriate option only for residual waste that cannot be biologically recovered.

    Taken together, the rubric indicates that cities seeking to maximize sustainability should prioritize composting and AD as the primary pathways for managing organic waste, while reserving WtE for non-organic residuals that cannot be feasibly recycled, composted, or digested. Future research should be done to better quantify the gains received from each of these solutions.

    Applying the Rubric to NYC
    NYC faces a structural mismatch between expanding organics collection and limited in-city processing capacity. DSNY has made meaningful progress so far, but the city lacks a coordinated processing strategy that aligns waste quality, facility type, and siting decisions. As a result, a significant share of organic waste will continue to be exported to landfills or regional waste-to-energy facilities, generating avoidable methane emissions, long-haul transportation impacts, and financial costs.

    The structure of NYC’s current waste system is largely a product of past historical decisions instead of a deliberate plan. After the closure of Fresh Kills Landfill back in 2001, the city shifted toward export-based disposal, transferring waste through long-haul trucking and rail into regional facilities. This reduced in-city landfill, but led to a more fragmented system with higher transportation costs and limited local processing, especially toward specific low-income neighborhoods.

    To address this gap, DSNY should adopt a sequenced, hybrid organics strategy that assigns distinct roles to composting, AD, and WtE. Composting should serve as the primary pathway for clean, source-separated residential organics, while anaerobic digestion should handle packaged and higher-contamination food waste streams. Thermal WtE should be limited to residuals only and excluded from future organics planning.

    Composting capacity should be expanded within city limits, with DSNY prioritizing enclosed, in-vessel facilities sited on underutilized municipal land, including select marine transfer stations, DSNY garage yards, and industrial-zoned parcels. Borough-specific composting facilities would help to reduce truck miles and improve system resilience, with local community composting gardens and networks playing a role in workforce development and public education. AD should be expanded at the local wastewater treatment plants, prioritizing expansion at existing Water Resource Recovery Facility (WRRFs) based on pre-processing. For the local communities that face this expansion, community engagement focuses on the jobs produced and how the local energy and digestate captured from AD will be reinvested back into the community. WtE should not be expanded or repositioned for organics, and instead continue to process residual waste after going through AD and composting. It will continue to provide diminishing climate and equity returns as the electric grid continues to decarbonize, and the focus should be on reducing waste as a whole.

    Implementing this hybrid strategy will require reliable public investment and coordination between government partners. Capital costs for upgraded infrastructure will rely on the capital budget, with DSNY remaining the lead agency implementing the projects and NYSDEC overseeing permitting and emissions compliance.

    All investments should also be paired with transparent monitoring and community governance. More granular and transparent data is critical, especially broken out by borough, building type – like residential, commercial, etc. – and capture rates. This helps DSNY to better optimize routes and where to target education and enforcement. It also helps identify where composting and pre-processing site locations are critical to success. A citywide siting study would allow DSNY to move from conceptual drawings to actionable planning. Additional research, either from NYC or from outside institutions, is required for the true scalability of AD. Modeling exactly how AD would work with other core wastewater treatment is important to understand with changes in climate change affected rainfall and flooding.

    Community impact and benefit-sharing mechanisms should also continue to be explored. The recommendation of this paper notes that equitable siting and localized benefits is crucial, but there isn’t much evidence on which model is best to ensure community trust and long-term acceptance. A better understanding about community oversight structures, revenue-sharing models, or other reinvestment strategies can help DSNY avoid repeating the same patterns of inequity.

    Conclusion
    Given this review, the recommendations for NYC’s organic waste program are the following:

    1. Composting and AD is the backbone of the system. Both technologies offer strong climate performance, clear circular value, and feasible infrastructure pathways when supported by targeted investment.
    2. NYC must invest in pre-processing and contamination control. Both composting and AD rely on clean organic waste, thus an in-city or nearby regional pre-processing hub would dramatically improve performance.
    3. AD should be expanded at wastewater treatment plants. Co-digestion offers a cost-effective, scalable path for increasing organics capacity without requiring new large-footprint facilities, but it must be done with community guidance and education.
    4. DSNY should prioritize siting decisions that reduce burdens to historically-impacted neighborhoods. Any improvements made without intentional governance reform will face strong pushback from the community.
    5. WtE should be restricted to residual waste only. Combustion is incompatible with NYC’s organics, soil, and equity-focused goals; it should not receive high-quality organics that could be composted or digested.

    Managing organic waste is central to any urban climate and sustainability strategy. Composting, anaerobic digestion, and thermal WtE all offer different strengths, limitations, and governance demands. Composting delivers the clearest circular benefits and lowest emissions when supported by community participation. AD adds renewable energy generation and integrates well with wastewater treatment systems, but requires capital-intensive infrastructure and precise operations. Thermal WtE, while reliable for residual waste, is poorly suited for organics.

    For dense cities like NYC, no single pathway is sufficient. A resilient and climate-aligned system must prioritize composting and AD for pre-processed organics and maintain strict contamination prevention, while limiting WtE to a narrow role for non-recyclable residuals. This blended approach strengthens circular material flows, reduces greenhouse gas emissions, and distributes environmental and economic benefits more equitably. In doing so, cities can shift away from a linear disposal model toward a more regenerative infrastructure system that supports long-term climate goals and community well-being.


    Major thank yous to the folks I interviewed including Arianna Cooper, William Flood, Jen McDonnall, and Lily Pollans; as well as the feedback and support provided by my professors Amy Kenyon & Raksha Vasudevan.
